title: System Design in a Hurry: Introduction
summary: What system design interviews assess, how they are structured, and how to use this track.
keyPoints: A system design interview measures how you navigate an open problem, not whether you match a hidden diagram.
Product prompts start from a user action; infrastructure prompts start from a shared capability.
Interviewers look for problem navigation, solution design, technical excellence, and communication.
Different requirements can justify different designs; defend your choices instead of searching for one right answer.
Senior answers add depth on scale, failure, and operational cost, and lead the deep dives.
Use the track in order, then practice the eight design scenarios against their rubrics.

complexity.note: Ask questions that change the design.
Cover one flow end to end.
Depth beats a list of technologies.
Treat the interviewer as a teammate.

commonMistakes: Starting with components before agreeing on users, scope, and constraints.
Reciting technologies without tying them to a requirement or failure mode.
Treating the first diagram as final and ignoring new constraints.
Saving all trade-offs and failure handling for the last two minutes.
interviewNotes: Say your assumptions out loud and note what would change if one is wrong.
Aim for a complete end-to-end flow before optimizing any one part.
Use one or two deep dives to show depth; breadth alone reads as shallow.
Practice with a timer so the structure becomes a habit.

checkYourself.question: What are the four assessment themes?
checkYourself.answer: Problem navigation, solution design, technical excellence, and communication and collaboration.

checkYourself.question: Why can two different designs both be correct?
checkYourself.answer: A prompt hides decisions such as scale, read-to-write ratio, consistency, and budget. Different answers to those questions justify different architectures.

checkYourself.question: How should you use the eight design scenarios?
checkYourself.answer: Attempt each one before reading the reference. Then compare your design with the checklist and rubric, note two gaps, and revisit the lessons that address them.
